chunks: The stupor of death and the regret of loss have surrounded them, so their limbs become languid and their complexion changes.

Then death increases its penetration among them, so one of them is prevented from speaking, although he lies among his family, looking with his eyes and hearing with his ears, with sound mind and intact intellect, pondering over how he wasted his life and in what he spent his time!

He recalls the wealth he collected, having blinded himself in seeking it, and acquired it from its clear and ambiguous sources. The consequences of its collection have clung to him, and he is on the verge of parting with it; it remains for those who come after him to enjoy and benefit from it, so it becomes an easy acquisition for others but a burden on his back.

The man's debts are tied to it, so he bites his hand in regret for what was disclosed to him about his affairs at the time of death. He becomes indifferent to what he coveted during the days of his life, and wishes that the one who envied him for it and felt jealous over it had acquired it instead of him!

key_terms.رُهُونٌ: Debts or pledges tied to wealth
key_terms.سَكْرَةُ الْمَوْتِ: The stupor or drowsiness of death

ai.seo_question: What is the regret of death regarding worldly wealth in Shia Islamic teachings?
ai.summary: In the context of Nahj al-Balagha’s eschatological discourses, this passage illustrates the 'sukrat al-mawt' (death pangs) as a moment of acute cognitive clarity where the soul remains tethered to the body, intensifying the regret over misallocated worldly pursuits. Shia scholars, such as Ibn Abi al-Hadid, emphasize this as a critique of materialism, highlighting how wealth accumulates 'liabilities' (tabi'at) that burden the deceased while becoming a source of pleasure for heirs, thus underscoring the transient nature of dunya versus the permanence of the akhirah.

en.sayed-ali-raza: Pangs of death and grief for losing (this world) have surrounded them. Consequently their limbs become languid and their complexion changes.

Then death increases its struggle over them. In some one it stands in between him and his power of speaking although he lies among his people, looking with eyes, hearing with his ears, with full wits and intelligence. He then thinks over how he wasted his life and in what (activities) he passed his time.

He recalls the wealth he collected when he had blinded himself in seeking it, and acquired it from fair and foul sources. Now the consequences of collecting it have overtaken him. He gets ready to leave it. It would remain for those who are behind him. They would enjoy it and benefit by it. It would be an easy acquisition for others but a burden on his back, and the man cannot get rid of it.

He would thereupon bite his hands with teeth out of shame for what was disclosed to him about his affairs at the time of his death. He would dislike what he coveted during the days of his life and would wish that he who envied him on account of it and felt jealous over him for it should have amassed it instead of he himself.
